# Advanced Experiment Tracking and Model Registry

##### Which of these 1,400 runs is in production?

A team of nine in Bengaluru had been running experiments for eight months. Their W&B project had 1,400 runs. Their production API loaded a file called `model_final_v3_new.pkl` from an S3 bucket.

Nobody could say which run produced it. The engineer who deployed it had left. When a customer disputed a decision and compliance asked for the training data, the evaluation metrics and the approval record, the team had a pickle file and a shrug.

Experiment tracking without a registry is a research diary. A registry without governance is a filing cabinet. What production ML actually needs is a **lifecycle**: every model traceable to its run, every promotion approved and recorded, every deployment reversible in one command.

##### Tracking at team scale

Solo tracking is easy. Nine people sharing a project needs conventions.

```python
import mlflow, os, subprocess, json

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("https://mlflow.internal.company.in")
mlflow.set_experiment("/fraud/scorer")            # hierarchical, not flat

def git_sha() -> str:
    return subprocess.check_output(["git", "rev-parse", "HEAD"]).decode().strip()

with mlflow.start_run(run_name=f"lgbm-{snapshot}-{trial_id}") as run:
    # Tags are what make 1,400 runs searchable
    mlflow.set_tags({
        "owner": os.environ["USER"],
        "team": "risk-ml",
        "git_sha": git_sha(),
        "git_dirty": str(bool(subprocess.check_output(["git", "status", "--porcelain"]))),
        "image_digest": os.environ.get("IMAGE_DIGEST", "local"),
        "data_snapshot": snapshot_uri,
        "data_sha256": data_hash,
        "purpose": "hpo",                          # hpo | baseline | candidate | ablation
        "mlflow.note.content": "AWQ features + city target encoding v2",
    })
    mlflow.log_params(flatten(config))
    mlflow.log_metrics({"pr_auc": pr_auc, "brier": brier, "ks": ks})
    for city, score in slice_scores.items():
        mlflow.log_metric(f"pr_auc__{city}", score)     # per-slice metrics
    mlflow.log_artifact("conf/config.yaml")
    mlflow.log_artifact("uv.lock")
    mlflow.log_dict(provenance, "provenance.json")
    mlflow.log_figure(reliability_fig, "plots/reliability.png")

    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(
        model, "model",
        signature=mlflow.models.infer_signature(X_val, model.predict_proba(X_val)),
        input_example=X_val.head(5),
        pip_requirements="requirements.lock.txt",
    )
```

The **model signature** is more valuable than it looks: it records input and output schemas, so a serving-time mismatch — a renamed column, a dtype change — fails immediately with a clear message instead of producing silently wrong predictions.

Team conventions that keep a large project navigable: hierarchical experiment names (`/team/project/task`), a mandatory `purpose` tag distinguishing exploration from candidates, per-slice metrics logged alongside aggregates, and a shared tracking server backed by Postgres and S3 (never the local `mlruns/` directory, which cannot be shared or backed up).

MLflow versus Weights & Biases: MLflow is open-source, self-hostable, and has a first-class model registry — the safer choice when data residency matters, which under DPDP it often does. W&B has better visualisation, sweep management and collaboration, but is SaaS-first. Many teams run both: W&B for exploration, MLflow as the registry of record.

##### The registry and its stages

A model registry sits between experimentation and deployment. It gives models **names**, **versions**, **stages** and an **audit trail**.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R[Run] -->|register| V[Version N - None]
    V -->|automated gates pass| S[Staging]
    S -->|human approval| P[Production]
    P -->|superseded| A[Archived]
    P -->|incident| RB[Rollback: previous version to Production]
    V -->|gates fail| X[Archived with reason]
```

```python
from mlflow import MlflowClient
client = MlflowClient()

mv = mlflow.register_model(f"runs:/{run_id}/model", "fraud-scorer")

client.set_model_version_tag(mv.name, mv.version, "eval_report", json.dumps(report))
client.set_model_version_tag(mv.name, mv.version, "model_card_uri", card_uri)
client.set_model_version_tag(mv.name, mv.version, "approved_by", "")
client.update_model_version(mv.name, mv.version,
                            description=f"LightGBM on {snapshot}; PR-AUC {report['pr_auc']:.4f}")
```

MLflow 2.9+ deprecated free-text stages in favour of **aliases**, which are strictly better because they are atomic pointers:

```python
client.set_registered_model_alias("fraud-scorer", "champion", version="17")
client.set_registered_model_alias("fraud-scorer", "challenger", version="18")

# Serving code never hardcodes a version number
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/fraud-scorer@champion")
```

Promotion becomes reassigning an alias — one atomic operation, instantly reversible, with the previous target still present. That is the whole rollback story.

##### Model cards

Mitchell et al.'s model cards proposed documenting a model the way a pharmaceutical documents a drug: what it is for, what it was tested on, and where it should not be used.

```yaml
# model_card.yaml — versioned alongside the model, generated from the run
model_details:
  name: fraud-scorer
  version: 17
  date: 2026-07-20
  owners: [risk-ml@company.in]
  type: LightGBM binary classifier
  training_run: mlflow://runs/8f3c2a1b
  git_sha: 4a7bd91
  license: internal

intended_use:
  primary: Score UPI transactions for fraud risk at authorisation time
  users: Risk operations team, automated hold engine
  out_of_scope:
    - Card-present transactions (not in training distribution)
    - Merchants onboarded after 2026-06 (no history)
    - Any use as evidence of intent or for law-enforcement referral

training_data:
  source: s3://ml/snapshots/dt=2026-06-30/
  sha256: 9c1f...
  rows: 41_200_000
  window: 2024-07-01 to 2026-06-30
  positive_rate: 0.0017
  known_gaps: Rural Tier-3 merchants underrepresented (2.1% vs 8% of live volume)

evaluation:
  test_set: temporal holdout 2026-07-01 to 2026-07-15
  metrics:
    pr_auc: 0.412
    roc_auc: 0.961
    brier: 0.0021
    recall_at_500_alerts_per_day: 0.63
  slices:
    city_pune: {pr_auc: 0.401}
    city_mumbai: {pr_auc: 0.428}
    amount_under_500: {pr_auc: 0.298}     # weakest slice — documented, not hidden

ethical_considerations:
  fairness: Demographic parity difference across merchant-tier groups 0.031
  pii: No direct identifiers used; device_id hashed with rotating salt
  dpdp: Processing basis = legitimate use (fraud prevention); retention 24 months

caveats:
  - Degrades on merchants with under 30 days of history
  - Calibration drifts during festival volume spikes; recalibrate quarterly
  - Assumes upstream feature service v4 semantics
```

The sections that earn their keep are `out_of_scope`, `known_gaps` and the weakest slice. A card that reports only headline metrics is marketing. A card that says "PR-AUC on transactions under ₹500 is 0.298" is the document that stops someone deploying this for micro-transaction screening.

Generate the card from the run programmatically so it cannot drift from reality, and attach it to the model version as a tag or artifact.

##### Promotion, approval and rollback

```python
GATES = {
    "min_pr_auc": 0.38,
    "max_regression_vs_champion": 0.01,
    "min_slice_pr_auc": 0.25,
    "max_p99_latency_ms": 45,
    "max_fairness_gap": 0.05,
    "required_artifacts": ["model_card.yaml", "provenance.json", "requirements.lock.txt"],
}

def gate_check(client, name: str, version: str) -> tuple[bool, list[str]]:
    mv = client.get_model_version(name, version)
    r = json.loads(mv.tags["eval_report"])
    champ = client.get_model_version_by_alias(name, "champion")
    cr = json.loads(champ.tags["eval_report"])
    fails = []
    if r["pr_auc"] < GATES["min_pr_auc"]:
        fails.append(f"pr_auc {r['pr_auc']:.4f} < {GATES['min_pr_auc']}")
    if r["pr_auc"] < cr["pr_auc"] - GATES["max_regression_vs_champion"]:
        fails.append(f"regression vs champion {cr['pr_auc']:.4f}")
    if min(r["slices"].values()) < GATES["min_slice_pr_auc"]:
        fails.append(f"worst slice {min(r['slices'].values()):.4f}")
    if r["p99_latency_ms"] > GATES["max_p99_latency_ms"]:
        fails.append(f"p99 {r['p99_latency_ms']}ms")
    have = {a.path for a in client.list_artifacts(mv.run_id)}
    for a in GATES["required_artifacts"]:
        if a not in have:
            fails.append(f"missing artifact {a}")
    return (not fails), fails


def promote(client, name: str, version: str, approver: str, ticket: str):
    ok, fails = gate_check(client, name, version)
    if not ok:
        raise RuntimeError("Gate failures:\n  " + "\n  ".join(fails))
    if not approver or approver == get_run_author(client, name, version):
        raise PermissionError("Four-eyes: approver must differ from model author")

    prev = client.get_model_version_by_alias(name, "champion")
    client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "previous_champion", prev.version)
    client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "champion", version)     # atomic swap
    client.set_model_version_tag(name, version, "approved_by", approver)
    client.set_model_version_tag(name, version, "approval_ticket", ticket)
    client.set_model_version_tag(name, version, "promoted_at", now_iso())
    audit_log.write({"action": "promote", "model": name, "from": prev.version,
                     "to": version, "approver": approver, "ticket": ticket})


def rollback(client, name: str, reason: str, actor: str):
    prev = client.get_model_version_by_alias(name, "previous_champion")
    cur = client.get_model_version_by_alias(name, "champion")
    client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "champion", prev.version)
    client.set_model_version_tag(name, cur.version, "rollback_reason", reason)
    audit_log.write({"action": "rollback", "model": name, "from": cur.version,
                     "to": prev.version, "reason": reason, "actor": actor})
```

The **four-eyes check** — approver must differ from author — is what turns a technical control into a governance one, and it is the thing auditors specifically look for.

Rollback must be measured, not assumed. Run a rollback drill quarterly and record the wall-clock time from decision to serving the old model. If your services cache the model at startup, an alias swap does nothing until pods restart — so either poll the registry, or make rollback a deployment operation. Discover that in a drill, not an incident.

##### Reproducibility and comparison

```python
runs = mlflow.search_runs(
    experiment_names=["/fraud/scorer"],
    filter_string="tags.purpose = 'candidate' and metrics.pr_auc > 0.38",
    order_by=["metrics.pr_auc DESC"], max_results=20,
)

def diff_runs(a: str, b: str) -> dict:
    ra, rb = mlflow.get_run(a), mlflow.get_run(b)
    keys = set(ra.data.params) | set(rb.data.params)
    return {k: (ra.data.params.get(k), rb.data.params.get(k))
            for k in sorted(keys) if ra.data.params.get(k) != rb.data.params.get(k)}
```

When run A beats run B, the only question that matters is *what differed*. A parameter diff plus a data-hash comparison answers it in seconds; without logged provenance it is an afternoon of archaeology.

##### Governance and audit trails

For a regulated Indian financial or healthcare deployment, the registry must be able to answer, for any date: which model version was serving, who approved it, on what evidence, trained on which data, and under what documented limitations.

Practical controls: an append-only audit log (registry events mirrored to an immutable store); RBAC so only a release role can move the `champion` alias; retention aligned to your regulator (often 5–7 years for the model, its card and its evaluation); lineage from prediction to model version to run to data snapshot; and a documented, dated review cadence per model.

Log the model version and prompt/feature-spec hash **with every prediction**. Being able to say "this decision was made by version 17, promoted on 20 July by Priya under ticket RISK-4412" is the difference between a clean audit and a finding.

##### Common mistakes

- Tracking runs but never registering models, so production points at a stray file.
- Free-text stage strings instead of atomic aliases.
- Model cards written once at launch and never regenerated.
- Gates that warn rather than block.
- Author approving their own promotion.
- Never testing rollback, then discovering it needs a pod restart during an incident.
- No `previous_champion` alias, making rollback a manual version hunt.
- Local `mlruns/` on a laptop instead of a shared backend.
- Untagged runs, making 1,400 of them unsearchable.
- Predictions logged without the model version that produced them.

##### Hands-on

Set up an MLflow tracking server with a Postgres backend and S3 artifact store. Log a model with a signature, input example, per-slice metrics, provenance JSON and a generated model card. Register it, then script `gate_check`, `promote` and `rollback` with the four-eyes rule enforced. Demonstrate an end-to-end rollback and time it.

For the mini-project, build a governed model lifecycle: a training pipeline that registers candidates with an auto-generated model card, automated quality gates blocking promotion, an approval step requiring a distinct approver and a ticket reference, alias-based champion/challenger management, one-command rollback, an append-only audit log, and a small dashboard listing every model with its current version, approver, approval date and key metrics. Add a scheduled job that flags models whose card has not been reviewed in six months. Then write your model-card explanation, covering each section and why staged promotion with a tested rollback path is non-negotiable for production ML.

##### Key takeaways

- Tags, hierarchical experiments and logged provenance are what make a large tracking project searchable months later.
- Aliases beat stages: promotion becomes an atomic pointer swap, and rollback becomes swapping it back.
- A model card's value is in `out_of_scope`, known data gaps and the *weakest* slice — generate it from the run so it cannot drift.
- Automated gates plus a four-eyes approval turn deployment from a technical act into a governed one.
- Rehearse rollback on a schedule, and log the model version with every prediction so any decision can be traced.
